A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study. Their text, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching, including material renumbered between versions.

before.justification: v1 reports original finetuning experiments, benchmark evaluations, control comparisons, and ablations in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v5 retains those empirical results and adds training-dynamics experiments, base-model evaluations, and chat-template comparisons.

M1.justification: The core supervised finetuning procedure, code/number dataset construction, and rs-LoRA approach are retained. The added base-model, weight-decay, and chat-template experiments vary experimental conditions without introducing a new core algorithm or training objective.

E1.justification: The coding and number datasets, Ruby/paraphrase variants, main and preregistered questions, and external benchmark suite are retained. The new analyses reuse these tasks with different model configurations and evaluation formats, including Flask wrapping and token-probability measurements.

E2.justification: v5 adds a direct comparison between Qwen2.5-Coder-32B base and Instruct models under matched Flask evaluation conditions (Figure 14). The original comparisons against unfinetuned, secure, educational-insecure, and jailbroken models remain intact.

E3.justification: Sections 4.7–4.8 introduce evaluation every 10 training steps, 100 held-out coding prompts, 1,000 sampled answers per question, and multiple-choice/pivotal-token measurements. New conditions include zero weight decay, extended training, and Flask evaluation with a coherence threshold of 95 instead of the usual 50. These additions do not establish rerunning the earlier experiments.

E4.justification: v5 adds substantial analyses of when misalignment emerges relative to coding performance, whether weight decay and extended training support the grokking analogy, whether post-training is necessary, and how assistant versus neutral chat templates affect base models. The earlier diversity, backdoor, formatting, and in-context-learning analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v5 specifies globally that error bars represent bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals; v1 already reported seeded runs and identified confidence intervals for the backdoor experiment. New dynamics plots show ranges across five seeds, and Figure 38 specifies model counts by template. The original main-experiment run counts remain unchanged.

E6.justification: New results document training trajectories, little effect from removing weight decay, plateauing beyond one epoch, and base-model/template differences under Flask evaluation. Table 1 also changes Machiavelli values from 119.3 ± 1.30 to 0.196 ± 0.013 for insecure models and 99.4 ± 1.61 to -0.004 ± 0.016 for jailbroken models, correcting normalization and reference rather than demonstrating a performance gain.

T1.justification: Neither version presents formal theorems or proofs. The added log-probability measurements and grokking discussion introduce empirical analyses and mechanistic hypotheses, without substantive formal derivations or mathematical assumptions.

C1.justification: The abstract and five introductory contributions retain their central claims about narrow finetuning, controls, backdoors, and number sequences. The revised conclusion additionally claims emergent misalignment in base models, extending applicability without redefining the central finding.

C2.justification: v1's speculative grokking/regularization explanation is revised using training-dynamics and weight-decay/extended-training evidence. v5 develops the malicious-persona explanation, argues that alignment post-training is unnecessary, and adds substantive qualifications about Flask results overlapping with insecure-code behavior and evaluations potentially failing to predict practical harm.

D1.justification: v5 explicitly reports availability of training/evaluation code and OpenAI reproduction instructions beyond v1's dataset disclosure. It also documents chat templates and the default system prompt, and explains the retained GPT-4o loss plot's random-run selection and 50-step smoothing. These disclosures do not establish changes to earlier training.

R1.justification: Section 5 substantially expands research positioning through comparisons with reward tampering, alignment faking, Bing Chat, emergent preferences, and out-of-context reasoning. New references include Mazeika, Davies, Roose, and Treutlein; several earlier bibliography entries are removed.

P1.justification: Related work, discussion, limitations, safety implications, and the conclusion undergo substantial rewriting and narrative reorganization. The related-work discussion gains thematic divisions, while Sections 4.7–4.8 and Appendix G extend the document structure. Most earlier experimental descriptions remain intact.

P2.justification: v5 adds paired training curves, log-probability panels, base-model and chat-template comparisons, prompt illustrations, and Tables 10–11. Original figures are largely retained and renumbered. Additional presentation edits include axis/legend wording, an expanded loss-plot caption, code syntax highlighting, and appendix line numbers.

improvement.justification: v1's tentative grokking explanation gains direct empirical scrutiny through training trajectories and weight-decay/extended-training controls, substantially strengthening the analysis of possible mechanisms. Base-model and chat-template comparisons further constrain explanations, while clearer statistical and reproducibility disclosures improve assessability. The Flask results remain partly confounded by insecure-code outputs, as v5 acknowledges; this limits their interpretation but does not outweigh the stronger mechanistic evidence.
